title: WHY DID PAUL MENTION ALEXANDER THE COPPERSMITH?
paragraphs: WHY DID PAUL MENTION ALEXANDER THE COPPERSMITH?

The name Paul carried into one of his final letters reveals something frightening about betrayal, something beautiful about forgiveness, and something every wounded Christian needs to understand before pain turns into poison.
There is a name sitting near the end of Paul’s final letter that almost feels out of place.
Alexander.
Not Peter.
Not John.
Not Timothy.
Not one of the heroes whose names Christians teach their children.
Alexander the coppersmith.
Paul is nearing the end of his race. He has already written words that sound almost like a man hearing eternity approaching:
“I have fought a good fight, I have finished my course, I have kept the faith.”
—2 Timothy 4:7, KJV
And then, surrounded by instructions, memories, loneliness, names of friends, and the approaching shadow of death, Paul remembers one man who hurt him.
He writes:
—2 Timothy 4:14–15, KJV
Why?
Why preserve Alexander’s name?
Why allow the memory of someone who wounded an apostle to remain in Holy Scripture for generations?
And perhaps the more uncomfortable question is this:
Why does Paul sound so different here from the sanitized version of Christianity many of us have learned to perform?
Because Paul does not say, “Nothing happened.”
He does not pretend Alexander was misunderstood.
He does not call evil good so that he can appear forgiving.
He names the harm.
And then he refuses to become its judge.
That distinction may save somebody reading this from becoming the very thing that wounded them.
The Greek is painfully direct:
“Ἀλέξανδρος ὁ χαλκεὺς πολλά μοι κακὰ ἐνεδείξατο· ἀποδώσει αὐτῷ ὁ κύριος κατὰ τὰ ἔργα αὐτοῦ.”
Alexandros ho chalkeus polla moi kaka enedeixato; apodōsei autō ho Kyrios kata ta erga autou.
Alexander the metalworker did Paul great harm; the Lord would render to him according to his works.

The word χαλκεύς (chalkeus) identifies Alexander as a smith or metalworker. Although traditionally rendered “coppersmith,” the term could be used more generally for someone who worked metal. The expression πολλά μοι κακά is equally difficult to soften: many evils, much harm, great injury done to Paul.
Paul was not imagining the wound.
He was not exaggerating forgiveness by denying reality.
Alexander hurt him.
That matters.
Because somewhere along the way, some Christians learned that forgiveness means pretending nothing happened.
Someone betrayed you?
Smile.
Someone lied about you?
Stay quiet.
Someone manipulated you?
Call it grace.
Someone repeatedly harms you?
Keep giving them unrestricted access because “Christians forgive.”
But that is not what Paul does.
Immediately after entrusting Alexander to God's judgment, Paul tells Timothy:
“Of whom be thou ware also.”
In Greek:
“ὃν καὶ σὺ φυλάσσου”
hon kai sy phylassou.
You also—guard yourself against him.
Read that again if you have spent years confusing forgiveness with unlimited access.
Paul can leave vengeance with God and still warn Timothy.
He can refuse personal retaliation and still recognize danger.
He can forgive without becoming foolish.
He can trust divine justice without pretending evil is harmless.
There is no contradiction.
There is maturity.
And maybe that is why Alexander’s name survived.
Not so Christians would spend two thousand years hating a man they never met.
But so wounded believers could learn what to do when another human being leaves damage behind.
There is something else we must handle carefully.

The New Testament mentions other men named Alexander. First Timothy 1:20 names “Hymenaeus and Alexander,” whom Paul says he delivered unto Satan that they might learn not to blaspheme. Acts 19:33 also mentions an Alexander during the Ephesian riot.
Was Alexander the coppersmith one of these men?
Possibly.
But Scripture does not explicitly tell us.
Interpreters have disagreed over the identification, and responsible reading should resist turning possibility into certainty.
We do not need speculation to make Paul's warning more dramatic.
What Scripture actually says is already devastating enough.
Alexander harmed Paul.
Alexander strongly opposed the apostolic message.
Timothy needed to be warned.
And judgment belonged to the Lord.
That last part changes everything.
“ἀποδώσει αὐτῷ ὁ κύριος”
apodōsei autō ho Kyrios.
“The Lord will repay him.”
Notice who is missing from the role of executioner.
Paul.
Paul does not say, “I will make Alexander pay.”
He says, in effect, “The Lord sees.”
There are wounds you cannot repair by getting even.
There are lies you cannot chase down fast enough.
There are people who may never apologize.
There are conversations where you will never receive closure.
There are betrayals where the person who destroyed your trust may continue living as though nothing happened.
And there is something terrifyingly seductive about revenge when you have been genuinely wronged.
You replay the conversation.
You imagine the day they finally understand what they did.
You want the truth exposed.
You want them embarrassed.
You want them to hurt just enough to understand your hurt.
Maybe you would never say it aloud.
But heaven has heard the conversations you have held inside your head.
Paul gives us another road.
Tell the truth about evil.
Protect others when protection is necessary.
Use wisdom.
Set appropriate boundaries.
But do not climb onto God's throne.
“The Lord will repay.”
Those words are not permission for vindictiveness.
They are liberation from it.
You do not have to become someone's judge in order for justice to exist.
God saw what happened when nobody else did.
God heard the conversation you could never prove happened.
God knows what was said behind the closed door.
God knows what was deliberately twisted.
God knows what it cost you.
And because He knows perfectly, you are free to surrender judgment perfectly to Him.
But the passage becomes even more astonishing when you keep reading.
After warning Timothy about Alexander, Paul writes:
—2 Timothy 4:16, KJV
Do you see it?
Alexander opposed him.
Others abandoned him.
Yet Paul's responses are not identical.
Concerning Alexander, Timothy needs a warning.
Concerning those who deserted him, Paul asks that their failure not be charged against them.
Biblical forgiveness is not moral blindness.
Grace has discernment.
Paul does not flatten every situation into the same category.
Some people were weak.
Alexander was actively dangerous.
Some needed mercy for abandoning him.
One needed to be watched.
That distinction matters enormously in real life.
The person who failed you in weakness is not necessarily the same as the person committed to harming you.
The friend who panicked is not necessarily the same as the manipulator who planned.
The believer who stumbled is not necessarily the same as the person who continues deliberately opposing truth.
Christian love does not require us to erase discernment.
And then comes perhaps the most beautiful sentence in the entire scene.
Paul has been harmed.
Paul has been opposed.
Paul has been deserted.
Human support disappears.
And he writes:
—2 Timothy 4:17, KJV
There it is.
That is the center.
Not Alexander.
Jesus.
Alexander may explain the wound.
Jesus explains why the wound did not win.
People left.
“The Lord stood with me.”
People weakened him.
The Lord “strengthened me.”
Someone opposed the message.
Yet Paul says the preaching continued through him.
This is Christianity at its deepest.
Not the promise that nobody will betray you.
Not the promise that faithful Christians never become lonely.
Not the promise that obedience protects you from malicious people.
The promise is Christ Himself.
When everybody else steps away, Christ does not.
When somebody drags your name through the dirt, Christ does not forget your name.
When your strength collapses, Christ remains.
When people leave you standing alone in the room you thought they would enter with you—
Jesus stands there.
Maybe your Alexander had another name.
Maybe it was someone you trusted.
Someone from church.
Someone you loved.
Someone you defended.
Someone you helped.
Someone who knew exactly where you were vulnerable because you were foolish enough—or loving enough—to let them close.
And maybe what hurts most is not merely what they did.
It is who did it.
Strangers can wound you.
But betrayal requires proximity.
Judas needed to be close enough to kiss Jesus.
Peter needed to know Jesus before denying that he knew Him.
The deepest wounds often come carrying familiar voices.
And this is where the Gospel confronts us.
Because eventually every wounded person faces a decision.
Will what they did to me determine who I become?
Paul's answer is no.
Not because the wound was imaginary.
Because Jesus was greater.
This is where Alexander's story unexpectedly brings us toward Calvary.
Jesus Christ knows betrayal more deeply than any of us.
He was betrayed for silver.
Abandoned by friends.
Denied by Peter.
Mocked.
Falsely accused.
Stripped.
Beaten.
Crucified.
And while hanging beneath the judgment our sins deserved, Christ was not merely giving humanity an inspiring example of endurance.
He was accomplishing redemption.
“For he hath made him to be sin for us, who knew no sin; that we might be made the righteousness of God in him.”
—2 Corinthians 5:21, KJV
At the cross, God does not pretend sin does not matter.
The cross proves how seriously God takes it.
And simultaneously, the cross reveals how unimaginably far His grace is willing to go to rescue sinners.
That includes people wounded by Alexanders.
And it includes people who have behaved like Alexander.
That second sentence is harder.
Because while reading this, perhaps you instinctively identified with Paul.
But what if you have been Alexander in somebody else's story?
What if you were the one who damaged them?
What if your words opposed truth?
What if you betrayed someone's confidence?
What if you destroyed a reputation?
What if the person reading Paul's warning and thinking of an enemy should actually be thinking of himself?
That is where Christianity becomes more than emotional therapy.
The Gospel does not exist merely to help victims feel stronger.
It calls sinners to repentance.
All sinners.
Including us.
You may have been betrayed.
You may also have betrayed.
You may have been lied about.
You may also have lied.
You may carry scars from someone else's sin while somebody else carries scars from yours.
And neither revenge nor denial can cleanse that.
Only Christ can.
The Gospel does not say, “You weren't that bad.”
It says something far more glorious.
You were guilty, and Christ died for sinners.
You were unable to save yourself, and the Son of God came for you.
You had a debt you could never repay, and Jesus carried sin to the cross.
He died.
He was buried.
He rose again.
And now forgiveness is offered not because sin was insignificant but because Christ's sacrifice is sufficient.
Repentance therefore is not humiliation without hope.
It is turning from sin toward the Savior whose grace is greater than your scandal.
That is why our message will always be:
Because Jesus rewrites everything.
Not by pretending the scandal never happened.
Not by editing evil out of your history.
Not by calling darkness light.
Jesus rewrites everything by redeeming sinners who could never rewrite themselves.
Look at Paul himself.
Before he became the wounded apostle warning Timothy about an opponent, Paul had been the opponent.
Before people persecuted Paul, Paul persecuted Christians.
Before Paul suffered for the name of Jesus, he tried to destroy those who called upon that Name.
Acts tells us Saul was “breathing out threatenings and slaughter against the disciples of the Lord.”
If Paul's biography had ended there, his name would have belonged to scandal.
Then Jesus met him.
Grace interrupted the story.
The persecutor became a preacher.
The enemy became an apostle.
The man who once tried to silence the Gospel eventually suffered because he refused to stop proclaiming it.
That is what Jesus does.
So perhaps the greatest lesson from Alexander is not, “Watch out for bad people.”
It is this:
Do not let another person's sin become the author of your remaining chapters.
Alexander did Paul harm.
But Alexander did not get Paul's ending.
Jesus did.
That may be the word somebody desperately needs tonight.
What happened to you was real.
But it does not own the ending.
What they called you does not own the ending.
What they exposed does not own the ending.
What you lost does not own the ending.
Even your own worst sin does not have to own the ending if you come to Christ in genuine repentance and faith.
Jesus Christ still saves sinners.
Jesus still restores.
Jesus still forgives.
Jesus still transforms.
Jesus still takes lives buried beneath shame and writes grace where everyone expected only scandal.
Maybe you have spent years secretly waiting for your Alexander to suffer.
Give the courtroom back to God.
Maybe you keep allowing a dangerous person into your life because you thought boundaries meant unforgiveness.
Remember Paul's words:
“ὃν καὶ σὺ φυλάσσου.”
Guard yourself.
Maybe you abandoned somebody when courage was required.
Repent.
Maybe you have been somebody else's Alexander.
Do not hide behind explanations.
Confess your sin.
Where appropriate and possible, seek reconciliation and make right what you can.
But above everything else, run to Christ.
There is mercy at His cross for repentant sinners.
There is cleansing for guilty consciences.
There is strength for wounded hearts.
There is freedom from revenge.
There is grace powerful enough to prevent yesterday's scandal from becoming tomorrow's identity.
Be honest.
There may be another believer reading the comments who needs to discover that they are not the only one still fighting.
And think of one person who needs this message.
Not someone you want to attack indirectly.
Someone you genuinely want to help.

Because eventually a name may come back into your mind, an old wound may reopen, or the temptation to retaliate may return. On that day, remember the imprisoned apostle who named the evil, warned his brother, surrendered judgment to God, and kept preaching Christ.
Supporting Gospel work can be one practical expression of generosity and partnership, though our first calling is always obedience to Christ—not allegiance to a page, platform, or ministry.
Invite your family.
Invite the friend who is struggling silently.
Invite the believer who has become spiritually cold.
Invite the seeker with difficult questions.
Invite even the person who does not yet believe.
Use them.
Share them.
Let truth travel farther than scandal.
Let Scripture travel farther than gossip.
Let the Gospel travel farther than the wound.
Because perhaps that is the final irony of Alexander the coppersmith.
He opposed Paul's words.
Yet nearly two thousand years later, we are still reading Paul's words.
Alexander could hurt the messenger.
He could not stop the message.
And neither can your Alexander.
The person who wounded you does not have enough authority to cancel what Jesus intends to do through a surrendered life.
So forgive without pretending.
Discern without becoming bitter.
Warn when love requires warning.
Repent when you discover Alexander in yourself.
Leave vengeance to God.
Stay near Jesus.
Keep preaching Christ.
Keep walking.
Keep loving.
Keep telling the truth.
And when everyone else disappears, remember the sentence Paul left behind for every lonely Christian who would someday wonder whether they could survive being abandoned:
“The Lord stood with me.”
Alexander may have been part of Paul's pain—but Jesus was the Author of Paul's ending.
